newsitem.title: UK: HORSE RACING-IRA CLAIMS GRAND NATIONAL BOMB WARNING.
newsitem.headline: HORSE RACING-IRA CLAIMS GRAND NATIONAL BOMB WARNING.

text.p: The Irish Republican Army (IRA) on Tuesday claimed responsibility for a bomb hoax which forced Britain's Grand National Horse race to be abandoned on Saturday.
The claim was made by a caller using a recognised IRA code word to Dublin's semi-state RTE broadcasting network.
RTE said the caller said such actions would not be needed if the Prime Minister John Major's British government adopted a constructive attitude to the Northern Ireland peace process.
He read out a statement which said: "The IRA were responsible for the disruption of the Grand National in England on Saturday.

"We remind John Major that, had he given as much importance to the negotiating of an end to the conflict in Ireland over the past few years as he attaches to the disruption of a single sporting event, a lasting peace settlement would have been closer and conflict and disruption a thing of the past."
Britain says the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, cannot take part in Belfast peace talks until the IRA calls a credible, permanent end to its war against British rule of Northern Ireland.
A caller using a recognised code word forced race organisers at Aintree to abandon the event. No bombs were found in a lengthy search of the track and surrounding area.
The hoax wrecked the holding of one of Britain's most cherished sporting events and one of the premier horse races in the world. It was re-run on Monday without incident.
The IRA action was seen by analysts as an attempt to force Northern Ireland on to the agenda of parties campaigning for British elections on May 1.

Sinn Fein, which shares the IRA goal of uniting Ireland under Dublin's rule, says it should be granted automatic access to the peace talks and that Britain should drop preconditions such as insisting that the IRA disarm.

Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Sir Patrick Mayhew, told journalists the Grand National incident and a spate of previous IRA attacks made chances of Sinn Fein qualifying for a talks place when they resume on June 3 more remote.
He said other groups at the talks, which are dominated by pro-British Unionist parties, would not negotiate with people "who are not committed to democracy."
Mayhew said there was no place for parties "which threaten to supplement their democratic mandate with Semtex (plastic explosive), bullets and mortars."
His words were clearly directed at the IRA, which 10 days ago tried to blow up a British army patrol in Northern Ireland and shot a policeman in the leg in a sniper attack.
Sinn Fein says it is a legitimate political party which won 15 percent of votes in the last provincial election and should be treated like any other party and allowed to negotiate at the talks.
But Britain says it cannot be admitted as long as it has a guerrilla army in the wings ready to attack or undermine any political settlement it does not like.
